newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's 3-yr-old Real Plan has to wait for growth.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's 3-yr-old Real Plan has to wait for growth.

text.p: Brazil's Real Plan, which will be three years old on July 1, will give the country low inflation and economic stability for years to come, but faster growth is not on the cards for now, Finance Minister Pedro Malan said.

"We want the kind of growth that is sustainable over time. That's what we've had since 1993, 1997 is our fifth year and 1998 will be our sixth," Malan told a gathering of businessmen in the Brazilian capital Tuesday.

Brazil's gross domestic product is expected to expand by three or 3.5 percent in 1997, a modest improvement on last year, but a rate way below expectations when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso took office in 1994, promising sweeping change.
Failure to get structural reforms through a conservative Congress have prevented the Cardoso administration from freeing the economy of the shackles of high interest rates and taxes.

"As long as we're running up (current account) deficits of $30 or $40 billion a year...it's hard to think of a significant reduction in taxes. And the same can be said for interest rates," Malan told the businessmen.
The minister, considered the hawk guarding the government's purse strings, said he was personally moved by the situation of Brazilian individuals and businesses suffering from the monetary squeeze.

"It's enough to stop one from sleeping at night," he said, but added that until Congress approved reforms of the pension system and the civil service and changed expensive labor laws, there would be no major upturn in the economy.
The lower house of Congress was due to resume voting on amendments to the civil service reform bill later Tuesday.

Political analysts believe reluctance among lawmakers to approve the bill, and the wide job cuts it implies, might mean it goes the same way as the pension reform bill which arrived in the Senate minus key points after a lower house rebellion.

Nearly a year on, and substantially rewritten, the pension reform bill was finally read to a Senate committee Tuesday. It might be put a vote in the panel next week and the first of two votes on the Senate floor seven days later, an official said.
It will also have to be approved again in the Chamber of Deputies.

Malan recognized a growing fear among investors that time was running out for approval of the reforms in the run-up to next year's presidential and congressional elections. Officials say the reforms will be unpassable by October this year, 12 months before election day.
Speaking about pension reform, Malan said: "I have no doubt that changes will be carried out by any future government because the system simply cannot go on as it is."
Brazil's pension system faces a deficit of up to $2.0 billion in 1997, a shortfall that is expected to rise steeply in coming years if no reform is carried out.

But Malan also said the popularity of the Real Plan, which cut annual inflation from 5,000 to ten percent in just three years, would give Cardoso an edge when he comes to seeking a new mandate to keep on reforming Brazil.
"I am certain there won't be a single candidate who gets on the electoral platform and says in clear terms that we should go back to the old days of high inflation," he said.
